# The Data

```{r}
#| label: preliminaries
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# load packages
library(tidyverse) 
library(knitr)
library(gtsummary)
library(ggstatsplot)
library(downlit)
library(broom)
library(here)

# load the data
df <- read_csv(here("data", "Simulated_BSED_Math_Research_Data.csv"))

df <- df |>
  mutate(
    Acad_Perf = factor(
      Acad_Perf, 
      levels = c("Satisfactory", "Good", "Very Good", "Excellent"), 
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )|>
  select(
    "Acad_Perf",
    "Year"
  )
```

## Relationship of Bsed-Math Students' Year Level to their Academic Performance

The Data Set is gathered from 69 students with 2 variable.

- `Acad_Perf` Satisfactory, Good, Very Good, Excellent.

- `Year` 1st Year, 2nd Year, 3rd Year, 4th Year.

This data set provides information on the relationships of Bsed-Math Students' Year Level to their Academic Performance, given that it is Satisfactory, Good, Very Good, Excellent based from their year level.

The first 6 rows of the data set are shown in @tbl-Acad_Pref.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-Acad_Pref
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| tbl-cap: "The first 6 observations of the data set."

df|>
  head() |> # getting the first six rows of the data
  kable(col.names = c("Academic Performance","Bsed-Math Students' Year Level")) # creating a table
```

## Descriptive Statistics

Academic performance is one of the variables examined in this study to determine the overall academic standing of BSED-Math students from first year to fourth year. The respondents are classified into four categories: Excellent, Very Good, Good, and Satisfactory. The frequency and percentage distribution will show how many students belong to each academic performance category and the proportion they represent in the total number of respondents. The results provide an overview of the academic performance of BSED-Math students across all year levels. The distribution of respondents among the different academic performance categories helps identify the most commonly reported level of academic achievement. It also provides an understanding of the general academic standing of the students, regardless of their year level.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Summary statistics of `Acad_Perf` when grouped according to `Year`."
#| message: false

df |> 
  tbl_summary(
    by = Year,
    include = Acad_Perf
  )
```
```{r}
df |>
  tbl_cross(
    row = Acad_Perf,
    col = Year,
    percent = 'column',
    margin = c("row","column"),
    label = list(
      Acad_Perf ~ "Academic Performance",
      Year ~ "Bsed-Math Students' Year Level"
    )
  )
```

# Hypothesis Testing

## Research Question

Relationship of Bsed-Math Students' Year Level to their Academic Performance?

## Hypothesis and Test Statistics

- $H_0:p_{year\,Level}-p_{Academic\,Performance}=0$; Bsed-Math Students' Year Level does not affect their Academic Performance.

- $H_a:p_{Year\,Level}-p_{Academic\,Performance}\ne0$; Bsed-Math Students' Year Level does affect their Academic Performance.

- Significance level, $\alpha=5\%\,\text{or p-value}\,\le\,.05$.

- **Pearson's** $\chi^2$-test of independence

- Independence.

- Expected counts: Not all expecter counts are $\ge 5$ (multiple cells fall below 5; see @tbl-expected). 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-expected
#| tbl-cap: Expected counts.

# Create contingency table
observed <- table(df$Year, df$Acad_Perf)

# Perform chi-squared test
chi_test <- chisq.test(observed)

# Extract the expected counts
expected <- chi_test$expected

# View expected counts
expected |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(
    " " = c("1st Year", "2nd Year", "3rd Year", "4th Year")
  ) |>
  relocate(" ", .before = 1) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2))) |>
  kable()
```

## Results and Interpretation

The bar chart and test statistics are shown on @fig-test.

```{r}
#| label: fig-test
#| fig-cap: Pie chart and test statistics.
#| fig-height: 3

ggbarstats(
  data = df,
  x = Year,
  y = Acad_Perf,
  type = "nonparametric",
  bf.message = FALSE,
  legend.title = "Bsed-Math Students' Year Level"
)
```
The results show a chi-square value of 9.26 with 9 degrees of freedom and a p-value of 0.41. Since the p-value (0.41) is greater than the 0.05 level of significance, the result is not statistically significant. Therefore, we fail to reject the null hypothesis. This indicates that there is no sufficient statistical evidence of a significant relationship between students' year level and their academic performance. Furthermore, the Cramér's V value of 0.02 indicates a negligible association between the two variables. This suggests that the relationship between year level and academic performance is very weak. Based on the descriptive results, the satisfactory category consists of 42% third-year students, while the good category has the highest proportion of first-year students at 50%. In the very good category, third-year students have the highest proportion at 38%. Meanwhile, among the excellent students, 60% are first-year students and 40% are third-year students. However, this category has only five respondents, so its percentages should be interpreted cautiously. Overall, the findings suggest that the year level of BSED-Math students is not significantly associated with their academic performance. Although there are some differences in the distribution of academic performance across year levels, these differences are not statistically significant. This implies that students' academic performance does not appear to be dependent on their current year level based on the data gathered from the 66 respondents.
